extracted.intended_audience: PR and communications professionals, GlobeNewswire users submitting press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for formatting press releases for distribution to media and the public, covering headline style, structure, tone, links, visuals, editing, and contact information to maximize engagement and media pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting your press release correctly is just as important as the content
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-structured document enhances engagement and attracts media interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat formatting as a core principle: correct structure and presentation make news more engaging, grab media attention and help your story shine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associated Press (AP) Style
rubrics_metrics.description: The Associated Press (AP) Style is the widely used standard for journalism and press releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow AP Style for headlines and text: capitalize only the first word and proper nouns in the headline. Begin the first paragraph with the dateline: city in all caps, state abbreviation, and the date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headlines should be specific, intriguing and informative
rubrics_metrics.description: Headlines should be specific, intriguing and informative, and keep the headline to less than 100 characters if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight the key point in your headline. Support it with a compelling subhead that shares another critical point. Keep headlines concise (under ~100 characters) to maximize clarity and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the inverted pyramid writing style
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep your press release organized using the inverted pyramid writing style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the most important information first, then add supporting details. Keep the body succinct—aim for three to six paragraphs in length; longer is not better. Prioritize readability and ensure the lead answers who/what/when/where/why/how.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overly promotional language; keep a factual tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using overly promotional language - press releases are factual and written with the media and public stakeholders in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write objectively and focus on newsworthiness rather than marketing copy. Use facts, data, and third-party validation (e.g., quotes) to support claims rather than superlatives or puffery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use subheadings, bullet points and quotes effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: How to use subheadings, bullet points and quotes effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subheads and bullet points to improve scannability and highlight key facts. Include quotes from subject matter experts to create trust with readers and provide human perspective; place them where they support the main points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linking policy and use of visuals
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard for the number of links in a press release is one link per 100 words; offer visuals with your press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive links—search engines may regard too many links as spam. Provide at least one relevant visual (images, video, or GlobeNewswire Media Snippets) to help bring the story to life and engage audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing and contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Check and double-check spelling and grammar; include contact information to make it easy for media reviewing the press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofread thoroughly for spelling, grammar and clarity. Provide clear contact details for media follow-up—at minimum include the name and title of the contact (and ideally phone/email). Make the contact easy to find in the release.
